title: Life of a Fabric GraphQL request
purpose: End-to-end request path from client and authorization through schema validation, source-backed resolution, typed response, and schema or mutation failure paths.
accessibleSummary: Life of a Fabric GraphQL request. GraphQL client request; Identity and permission gate; Parse and validate schema; Resolve source operation; Typed JSON response; Mutation and agent branches; Schema and workload risks.
longDescription: End-to-end request path from client and authorization through schema validation, source-backed resolution, typed response, and schema or mutation failure paths.

nodes.label: GraphQL client request
nodes.summary: A client sends a query or mutation selecting fields from the published API schema.
nodes.detail: The selection set expresses exactly which typed fields the caller requests.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client contract starts at the schema, not at database-specific SQL.

evidence.note: Fabric API for GraphQL exposes a typed GraphQL endpoint over supported data sources.

drill.example: An app requests customer id, name, and open orders.
failureModes: A client requests a field removed from the schema.

nodes.label: Identity and permission gate
nodes.summary: The endpoint evaluates caller authentication and access before resolving data.
nodes.detail: API access does not bypass permissions on the configured Fabric data source.
nodes.whyItMatters: The gate keeps a convenient API surface from becoming an alternate authorization path.

evidence.note: GraphQL requests use Fabric authentication and authorization for endpoint and source access.

drill.example: An application service principal calls an endpoint it was granted access to.
failureModes: Endpoint access is granted more broadly than underlying data.

nodes.label: Parse and validate schema
nodes.summary: The service parses the document and validates fields, types, and operation shape against its schema.
nodes.detail: Invalid selections stop before source execution and return GraphQL errors.
nodes.whyItMatters: Early validation makes schema evolution visible to clients.

evidence.note: Fabric generates a GraphQL schema from configured source objects for typed querying.

drill.example: A misspelled orderStatus field fails validation without querying the warehouse.
failureModes: Source schema changes invalidate a client selection.

nodes.label: Resolve source operation
nodes.summary: Resolvers translate validated fields into operations against the configured source.
nodes.detail: Filtering, projection, and relationship traversal are pushed toward the data source where supported.
nodes.whyItMatters: Resolver behavior determines both correctness and source workload.

evidence.note: The API resolves GraphQL queries against configured Fabric data sources.

drill.example: The customer selection resolves through a SQL analytics source.
failureModes: An unbounded selection creates excessive source work.

nodes.label: Typed JSON response
nodes.summary: Resolved values are assembled into GraphQL data and error envelopes.
nodes.detail: The response shape follows the client's selection and can contain field-level errors.
nodes.whyItMatters: A stable typed contract decouples consumers from physical table access.

evidence.note: GraphQL returns typed API results shaped by the requested selection.

drill.example: The app receives only customer id, name, and open orders.
failureModes: Partial errors are ignored by the client.

nodes.label: Mutation and agent branches
nodes.summary: Mutations change supported source data; agents are a separate grounded conversational access pattern.
nodes.detail: Treat write operations and natural-language agent requests as distinct contracts with distinct controls.
nodes.whyItMatters: Separating branches prevents GraphQL from being described as an AI reasoning layer.

processing: Apply write controls or route through an agent's grounding
drill.example: An app updates a supported record, while a data agent answers a business question through its own tools.
failureModes: Conflating API permissions with agent grounding policy.

nodes.label: Schema and workload risks
nodes.summary: Schema drift, over-broad selection, and unsupported operations can break or overload clients.
nodes.detail: Contract tests and bounded queries catch failure before a production consumer is affected.
nodes.whyItMatters: The warning makes API lifecycle ownership explicit.

evidence.note: The generated schema reflects configured source objects, so source and API evolution must be managed together.

drill.example: CI detects a renamed source column before the mobile app deploys.
failureModes: Breaking schema change reaches production without client coordination.
